Items.Authors: Miguel Santos, Carlos M. Correia, Ana Sequeira
Items.Title: Finding exo-Earths and potentially life elsewhere: the need for extreme adaptive optics systems
Items.Abstract: The European Extremely Large Telescope (E-ELT) will rely on the Planetary Camera and Spectrograph (PCS) to detect and study exoplanets, demanding an exceptionally fast and precise extreme adaptive optics (XAO) system. This work presents a machine-learning approach designed to ease these real-time control requirements of the PCS.

Items.Authors: Pierre Royer, Leonardo Peri, Wim De Munter, Gert Raskin, Julien Storm, Bart Vandenbussche, Tjorven Delabie, Camille Pirat, Maddalena Reggiani, Hugues Sana, Mikel Samson, Louis Storm, Dirk Vandepitte, Sibo Van Gool, Rhimas Van de Putte, Bram Vandoren, Dominic Bowman
Items.Title: Fine-guidance sensor image simulation and pointing performance assessment for the CubeSpec mission
Items.Abstract: CubeSpec is a 12U CubeSat scheduled for launch in 2027 as an in-orbit demonstrator for high-resolution astrophysical spectroscopy. With a pointing stability expected to be around 1 arcmin, its excellent attitude determination and control system (ADCS) remains to ensure the targets remain focussed in the 2.5 x 6.5 arcsec entrance slit of the spectrograph.    CubeSpec therefore incorporates a secondary pointing subsystem, the High Precision Pointing Platform (HPPP), which employs a closed-loop tip–tilt mirror coupled with a dedicated fine-guidance sensor (FGS). Accurate modelling of the FGS response is essential for predicting the achievable pointing performance.    In this paper, we present an image-simulation tool developed for the FGS, together with a performance assessment of the HPPP. The analysis combines simulated sensor data with hardware test results obtained at both the ADCS and HPPP levels, providing an end-to-end evaluation of the system’s expected on-orbit behaviour.

Items.Authors: Wayne H. Baumgartner, Gianluigi De Geronimo, Jarred M. Roberts, Nabin Poudyal, Wesley Hodge, Valter Bonvicini, Terri Brandt, Sukanya Chakrabarti, Yuri Evangelista, Marco Feroci, Martin Grim, Paul Ray, Eric Wulf, Gianluigi Zampa
Items.Title: First detector results using the new Naval Research Laboratory NSX1 ASIC developed for X-ray coded mask imagers with large area SDDs
Items.Abstract: The NSX1 ASIC is a 64-channel low noise and low power device developed for use with large area silicon X-ray detectors such as the Wide Field Monitor coded mask instrument on the Strobe-X Xray Probe mission concept. The first ASICs were fabricated, delivered and tested in 2025, with early tests showing good ASIC performance of the standalone device, meeting its design goal with a measured noise performance of 5 e- ENC. We report here on the first tests of the ASIC coupled to a Silicon Drift Detector. For these tests we used a single pixel hexagonal SDD 4 mm on a side and 450 um thick connected to one of the ASICs 64 channels.

Items.Authors: Woojin Kim, Bongkon Moon, Dukhang Lee, Dae-Hee Lee, Minsup Jeong, Yunjong Kim, Jihun Kim, Seonghwan Choi, Jehyuck Shin, Seul-Min Baek, Mingyeong Lee, Sung-Joon Park, Chae Kyung Sim
Items.Title: Flight Model development and system verification of the GrainCams payload for the CLPS lunar rover
Items.Abstract: The Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, a component of NASA’s Artemis program, supports lunar exploration by enabling the delivery of scientific instruments to the Moon through commercial lander missions. GrainCams is a candidate payload developed by the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI), consisting of SurfCam and LevCam to study micro-scale regolith structures and lofted dust near the lunar surface. This presentation introduces the objectives and system design of GrainCams, highlighting its role in advancing surface science investigations on future lunar exploration missions.

Items.Authors: Maria Begoña García-Lorenzo, Seifeldin Abouelella, José A. Acosta-Pulido, Kabir Baig, Julio A. Castro-Almazán, Antonio Eff-Darwich, Zenaida García-Rodríguez, Kshitij Ghimire, Moisés Pulido Torres, Alejandro Trujillo-Ramos
Items.Title: Focal-plane diagnostics of atmospheric and dome-induce turbulence: exploring techniques and applications
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence limits image quality in ground-based astronomy. Its impact depends on the overall turbulence strength, the wavefront spatial-coherence outer scale (L₀), and turbulence generated inside the telescope enclosure. While seeing and related parameters are routinely monitored, measurements of L₀ and dome turbulence remain scarce.  We build on recent methodology for seeing-limited integral-field data to show how spatial information in spectroscopic observations can be used to diagnose these effects. We investigate: (1) extracting L₀ from wavelength-dependent spatial profiles in long-slit spectroscopy; (2) using AO-assisted MUSE data to estimate the residual outer scale and assess dome turbulence; and (3) constructing data-driven 3D PSF models for deconvolving IFS data obtained under natural seeing.

Items.Authors: Adam B. Johnson, Christian Marois, Olivier Lardière, William Thompson, Joeleff Fitzsimmons, Dylan Kerr, Andre Fogal, Kaitlyn Hessel, Christoper Mann, Darryl Gamroth, Angus Bews, Scott MacDonald, Alan McConnachie, Julien Lozi, Olivier Guyon, Garima Singh, Matthew Wung, Naoyuki Tamura
Items.Title: From Canada to Maunakea: shipping, commissioning, and practical insights from deploying the fully assembled SPIDERS instrument on the Subaru Telescope
Items.Abstract: We report the logistics for transporting the fully assembled SPIDERS instrument from Canada to Subaru Telescope. This required coordinated scheduling between remote teams, customs and border preparation, and management of controlled goods, lasers, chemicals, and batteries. To protect sensitive hardware and alignment during truck, air, sea, and on-mountain transport, the instrument used wire-rope isolators in a crate designed for controlled lifting and handling. Custom three-axis shock loggers and environmental monitors recorded acceleration, temperature, humidity, and pressure while contamination controls preserved optical cleanliness. Real-time tracking aided response to delays, and secure retention of optics and fasteners limited vibration-induced shifts. These measures enabled rapid unpacking, alignment, and verification on arrival, ensuring that SPIDERS reached Subaru ready for commissioning as a high-contrast imager and spectrograph using focal-plane wavefront sensing behind AO3k.

Items.Authors: Massinissa Hadjara, Hangxin Ji, Qinyang Dong, Mustapha Meftah, Bernard Foing
Items.Title: From early concepts to lunar hypertelescopes: roadmap for next-generation optical astronomy on the Moon
Items.Abstract: We present a historical and technical roadmap tracing the evolution of concepts that lead toward future lunar hypertelescopes for ultra-high-resolution optical astronomy. Building on diluted-aperture and interferometric concepts, we exploit recent progress in formation flying, precision metrology and lunar surface operations. The Moon offers unique advantages: seismically quiet ground, no atmosphere, cold traps for cryogenics, and long-term infrastructure potential. These enable sparse to kilometric baseline arrays far beyond Earth-based limits. We review paths from near-term precursor interferometers (10–100 m class) to large hypertelescope networks achieving milli- to micro-arcsecond resolution for direct imaging of exoplanets, stellar surfaces, and compact objects. Key milestones, scientific drivers, and engineering challenges are identified to evolve from current studies toward permanent lunar optical interferometric facilities.

Items.Authors: Massinissa Hadjara, Hangxin Ji, Qinyang Dong, Anton Pomazan, Jinghui Zheng, Yindun Mao, Leonardo Cament, Martin Adams, Marcos Diaz, Rene Mendez, Bernard Foing, Mustapha Meftah, Rabah Ikhlef, Djounai Baba-Aissa
Items.Title: From Earth’s harshest landscapes to lunar horizons: engineering telescopes for extreme environments
Items.Abstract: We present a comparative engineering roadmap for optical telescopes designed to operate in extreme environments on Earth and the lunar surface, particularly for investigating small Solar System bodies. Drawing on lessons from high-altitude deserts, polar stations, and remote platforms, we propose solutions for lunar-based telescopes to monitor near-Earth space, increase detectability of near-Earth asteroids (NEAs), and improve follow-up. These telescopes will also observe transient phenomena like gamma-ray bursts, supernovae, and variable stars, while providing data on space weather and radiation. The Moon’s stable platform, lack of atmosphere, and continuous observing windows offer unique advantages for long-term monitoring of NEAs, space debris, and other celestial phenomena. This project outlines engineering concepts for precursor lunar telescopes and discusses milestones for transitioning from Earth-based systems to robust, autonomous lunar implementations for continuous operation.

Items.Authors: David Sanmartim, Alysha Shugart, Anastasia Alexov, Bruno Quint, Eric Christensen, Erik Dennihy, Kevin Fanning, Kshitija Kelkar, Paulina Venegas, Yijung Kang
Items.Title: From issues to insight: a Jira analytics dashboard to prioritize and manage work during Rubin Observatory commissioning and operations
Items.Abstract: Large observatories accumulate thousands of Jira issues across hardware, software, integration, and procedural work, yet native Jira dashboards remain project-scoped and offer limited support for cross-system triage. We present a lightweight analytics dashboard that turns Jira into an observatory-scale decision-support and triage tool for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. It converts the unstructured pool of tickets into concise views that highlight where problems cluster, which work is most urgent, and how load is distributed. The paper will describe the dashboard’s architecture and configuration, and provide examples of fault localization, workflow, and workload views used in Rubin commissioning and operations to make triage more efficient and surface bottlenecks earlier. We also outline how other teams can adapt the approach to their own Jira projects by remapping fields and hierarchies, turning the issue tracker into a practical tool for daily operations and backlog governance.

Items.Authors: Windell Tanaka
Items.Title: From lab prototype to autonomous flight system: robust on-sky and in-flight performance of the ERIN star camera for the PUEO balloon mission
Items.Abstract: The Equatorial Reference Imager for Navigation (ERIN) is the autonomous star camera for the Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO) long-duration balloon mission. Our previous paper described the hardware and initial lab tests; here we report its maturation into a flight-ready subsystem and its on-sky and in-flight performance.    We summarize the updated software pipeline, including localized background subtraction, robust source detection, a combined autoexposure/autogain controller, and autofocus using image-contrast and diameter metrics. We also outline the interface to the onboard star-pattern solver and pointing system.    Results from the Antarctic flight will be presented, including solve rate and latency, sky coverage versus solar elevation, attitude accuracy versus independent references, stability of autogain and autofocus loops, representative flight images, and thermal and power behavior of the star-camera subsystem.

Items.Authors: Alejandro S. Farah Simon, Carolina Keiman, Joel Sanchez-Bermudez, Salvador Cuevas , Fernando Ángeles Uribe, Rubén Flores-Meza, Valente Vázquez, Rebeca García-López, Gerhard Ulbricht
Items.Title: From reverse engineering to manufacturing: Finite-Element cryogenic and optomechanical validation of the GRAVITY+ Grism System
Items.Abstract: GRAVITY+ is an upgrade of the VLTI GRAVITY instrument aimed at extending sensitivity to fainter astronomical targets while improving high-contrast performance on bright objects. This contribution presents the reverse-engineering, dimensional verification, and optomechanical validation activities carried out to integrate a new germanium grism into the GRAVITY grism wheel. Finite-element simulations were performed to assess the thermal behavior of the optomechanical assembly under cryogenic conditions, and cryogenic tests were conducted in the Colibrí cryostat at IA-UNAM to validate mechanical stability and alignment.

Items.Authors: Emaad Paracha, Steven J. Benton, Aurelien A. Fraisse, Ajay S. Gill, John W. Hartley, Bradley Holder, William C. Jones, Lun Li, Thuy Vy T. Luu, Richard J. Massey, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Johanna M. Nagy, C. Barth Netterfield, Susan F. Redmond, Jason D. Rhodes, L. Javier Romualdez, Jurgen Schmoll, Sayan Saha, Bryce Warren, Ben Boyd, Jason Brown, Peter Bartosik, Pablo Trujillo, Philippe Voyer
Items.Title: From sky to screen: improving downlinking over error-prone omni-directional links from the stratosphere
Items.Abstract: Long-duration stratospheric balloon missions must transmit large volumes of scientific and telemetry data over variable, omni-directional links prone to packet loss and bandwidth fluctuations. To address this, we developed a semi-autonomous file-downlink system for high-altitude astronomy missions such as SuperBIT and its successor, GigaBIT. The system comprises a payload client, ground server, and cleaner program capable of operating across UDP and TCP links. The client manages a dynamic queue of data and divides them into fixed-size chunks with metadata, enabling resumable transfers and selective retransmissions. This chunk-level approach ensures only corrupted data is resent, reducing bandwidth usage. The system helps increase overall throughput, substantially improving telemetry downlink in constrained stratospheric telescope missions. This talk presents the system design and protocol behaviour, along with the performance during SuperBIT’s final flight.

Items.Authors: Norman Diaz, Braulio Cancino, Patricio Cortes, Manuel Gomez, Craig S. Lage, Fritz Mueller
Items.Title: From unstable to reliable: Dome shutter control system upgrade for the Rubin Observatory Auxiliary Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Auxiliary Telescope (AuxTel) dome shutter at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is essential for protecting sensitive optics and enabling remote operations. The original shutter control system suffered from multiple reliability issues, including random activations, unstable communication, and weak hardware design, which posed risks to uninterrupted science operations. Over one year of analysis and engineering intervention, six major issues were systematically addressed through firmware refactoring, FPGA-based control, industrial-grade wireless communication, and hardware reinforcement with redundancy and power backup. The upgraded system now achieves a Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) exceeding 42,000 hours and is projected to operate reliably for over 10 years. This work demonstrates the critical role of reliability engineering in observatory infrastructure and provides lessons applicable to similar dome and shutter systems worldwide.

Items.Authors: Cihan Tugrul Tezcan, Ahmet Emin Kan, Muhammed Baki Bayram, Onur Şatır, Cahit Yeşilyaprak
Items.Title: full robotic transformation of the DAG-turbulence profiling station (DAG-TPS) for autonomous atmospheric monitoring
Items.Abstract: The DAG-Turbulence Profiling Station (DAG-TPS) monitors atmospheric turbulence using simultaneous DIMM and MASS-DIMM measurements. Although originally operated remotely, it still required human interaction, limiting continuity and efficiency. This study introduces the full robotic conversion of the system, including autonomous scheduling, environmental-awareness logic, fault-tolerant operation, and hardware upgrades for reliable unattended use. Early tests show major improvements in temporal coverage and data consistency, enabling continuous turbulence characterization at the DAG Observatory and providing a foundation for future adaptive-optics planning.

Items.Authors: Mario De Lucia, Paolo Dal Bo, Giovanni Signorelli, Andrea Tartari, Andrea Moggi, Andrea Passerini, Andrea Limonta, Graeme Smecher, Jean-François Cliche, Joshua Montgomery, Kateryna Leonova, Mario Zannoni, Matt Dobbs, Maurizio Massa, Michele Pinchera, Stefano Della Torre, Tommaso Lari, Donato Nicolo
Items.Title: Functionality and performance of the upgraded design of the LiteBIRD SQUID Controller Unit in a full read-out chain
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a spaceborne telescope scheduled for launch in the 2030s to measure the polarization anisotropies of the CMB and provide high sensitivity polarization maps with unprecedented frequency coverage. A likely option for the readout chain involves a dual-stage SQUID amplification in order to meet the SNR and the thermal-budget requirements .It uses a front-end SQUID placed close to the detectors to provide a small gain while decoupling the TES bias circuit from the readout impedance. A second SQUID provides the high-gain amplification and can be located on a warmer stage with less constraints on power dissipation.  The new SQUID Controller Unit design addresses the issue of operating two cascaded SQUIDs and has been modified in order to match thermo-mechanical requirements in view of TRL6 qualification. In this work, we report on the ongoing development of the control electronics for the DSS and we show the first end-to-end performance test of the complete readout chain.

Items.Authors: José M. Filgueira, Jordi Molgó, Marianne Cox, Jorge Barrios
Items.Title: GMT Integrated Adaptive Optics RTC Design and Prototype - New Technology Challenges and Opportunities.
Items.Abstract: The next generation of Extreme Large Telescopes (ELTs) will incorporate Adaptive Optics as an integral component of their wavefront control system. In this paper, we present the progress made in designing and implementing a prototype of an Integrated Adaptive Optics Real Time Computer (RTC) for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). We conducted a comprehensive requirements analysis to validate that the prototype is able to achieve the necessary compute throughput, bandwidth (both memory and network), and storage to meet the higher-level end-to-end loop latency and telemetry requirements.

Items.Authors: Sanghyuk Kim, Woojin Park, Chan Park, Sungho Lee, Heeyoung Oh, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Sang-Mok Cha, Ueejeong Jeong, Gregory N. Mace, Cynthia B. Brooks, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Cooper W. Dix, Alycia J. Weinberger, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: mechanical design strategy for the MagNIFIES pathfinder on Magellan Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS) is a first-generation near-infrared spectrograph for GMT, providing high-resolution (R ≈ 65,000–80,000) spectroscopy over 1.08–5.40 μm. We plan to develop the Magellan Near-IR Five-band Immersion grating Efficient Spectrograph (MagNIFIES) as a natural-seeing pathfinder instrument for the Magellan telescope prior to GMT's completion. MagNIFIES offers the same wavelength coverage but with slightly lower resolving power (R ≈ 45,000-65,000). The two instruments share the optical design for the spectrograph, with differences in foreoptics, slit size, electronics, software, and the telescope interface. Because of the reduced mass limit on the Magellan Nasmyth rotator, we discuss a mechanical design strategy for using the same cryostat while reducing the mass and satisfying the requirements of both instruments. We present the the thermal budget calculations and analysis results for the revised mechanical design.

Items.Authors: Woojin Park, Sanghyuk Kim, Heeyoung Oh, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Gregory Mace, Ueejeong Jeong, Hanshin Lee, Sungho Lee, Chan Park, John M. Good, Cynthia Brooks, Sang-Mok Cha, Bi-Ho Jang, Alycia J. Weinberger, Cooper W. Dix, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: preliminary mechanical design of pupil rotator for a cryogenic near-infrared spectrograph
Items.Abstract: We present the preliminary mechanical design of a pupil rotator developed for the Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS). In the infrared, thermal radiation and scattered light from outside of the clear aperture of the primary mirror introduces significant background noise. To mitigate this effect, a mask is placed at the pupil plane to block unwanted light. We present the preliminary mechanical design of a pupil rotator developed for GMTNIRS. The system comprises a pupil mask, worm gear assembly, cryogenic motor, hall effect sensor for home positioning, and a gearbox. The mask matches the geometry of the GMT primary mirror segments. Finite element analysis was conducted to calculate a spring and flexure preloads and to estimate the operating temperature of the pupil mask. We also present a prototype pupil rotator equipped with a warm stepper motor, which is being operated at room temperature prior to cryogenic testing.

Items.Authors: Heeyoung Oh, Sanghyuk Kim, Woojin Park, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Ueejeong Jeong, Sungho Lee, Chan Park, Jae-Rim Koo, Jae Sok Oh, Sang-Mok Cha, Hyeon Cheol Seong, Bi-Ho Jang, Jae-Joon Lee, Ho-Gyu Lee, Gregory N. Mace, Cynthia B. Brooks, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Cooper Dix, Alycia J. Weinberger, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: prototyping and test
Items.Abstract: We present the prototyping and experimental activities for the development of the Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS). GMTNIRS is an advancement beyond its predecessor, the Immersion Grating Infrared Spectrometer (IGRINS), and its extended wavelength coverage to 5.4 µm makes thermal-radiation control a critical aspect of the design. The operating components of GMTNIRS are seven H2RG detectors, electronics and control systems compliant with GMT requirements through an EtherCAT-based architecture, and a cryogenic pupil rotator. These efforts also support the MagNIFIES project, enabling earlier application of GMTNIRS capabilities on a Magellan Telescope. Comprehensive verification plan matrix has been developed, and a dedicated test chamber has been manufactured to validate key instrument aspects, including thermal control, radiation shielding, and customized detector cabling. This presentation will share the overall prototyping plan and early results.

Items.Authors: Quentin Fournier, Guillaume Bourdarot, Frank Eisenhauer, Helmut Feuchtgruber, Dieter Lutz, Stefan Gillessen, Reinhard Genzel, Taro T. Shimizu, Felix Mang, Michael Hartl, Thomas Ott, Ekkehard Wieprecht, Julien Woillez
Items.Title: GRAVITY+ upgrade: reducing non-common-path aberrations for 10 μas astrometric accuracy
Items.Abstract: Gravity is a state-of-the-art instrument for astrometric infrared interferometry. In its phase-referenced dual-field mode, it routinely achieves better than 50 μas accuracy, ultimately limited by systematic errors not compensated by dual-field metrology. These non-common-path aberrations mainly arise from high-order signatures caused by optical defects in the current fiber couplers. As part of the GRAVITY+ upgrades, we present the development of the upgrade of GRAVITY Fiber Coupler, which includes installing high-precision mirrors designed for nanometer-level surface quality. We introduce laboratory metrology results from the integration of these mirrors in a fiber coupler replica and the validation of interferometric tools diagnosing the metrological wavefront with nanometer accuracy, demonstrating readiness for on-site integration. This operation, expected at the end of 2027, will enable 10 μas astrometric accuracy in dual-band mode with only a few minutes of integration time.

Items.Authors: Jules Fowler, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Maaike van Kooten, Maïssa Salama, Antonin Bouchez, Avinash Surendran, Charlotte Guthery, Eduardo Marin, Mahawa Cissé, Max Service, Charlotte Bond, Will Gauvin, Emiel Por
Items.Title: Ground control to major time-lag: on-sky results of predictive wavefront control at Keck Observatory
Items.Abstract: Directly imaging and characterizing exoplanets requires extreme adaptive optics (XAO), to achieve exquisite wavefront correction over a small field of view. Predictive wavefront control (PWFC) mitigates temporal errors (often a leading term in these XAO systems) by predicting where the wavefront will be by the time the system correction is applied. In particular, empirical orthogonal functions (EOF) learn correlations in a wavefront using wavefront sensor history. We present on-sky results of a new implementation of EOF built directly into the Keck-II real time controller (RTC). This work revitalizes previous PWFC work at Keck, by showing improved performance over an integral controller during on-sky observing. Finally, we discuss optimization strategies for EOF on sky. This work not only improves current observing for the Keck community, but also acts as a pathfinder for predictive control methods with extremely large telescopes.

Items.Authors: Mark A. Mueller, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Sagi Ben-Ami, Isaac Anderson, Daniel Baldwin, Daniel Durusky, Ofir Hershko, Colby A. Jurgenson, Kenneth McCracken, Heeyoung Oh, Jae Sok Oh, Cem Onyuksel, William Podgorski, Chan Park, Matthew Smith, Yahel Sofer Rimalt, Abigail Unger, Joseph Zajac
Items.Title: Hardware fabrication update for the GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF)
Items.Abstract: The GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) is a fiber-fed, optical echelle spectrograph that will be a first light instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). G-CLEF is a general-purpose echelle spectrograph with precision radial velocity (PRV) capability. We will design and build an interim installation configuration for G-CLEF at Magellan’s 6.5m Clay telescope. This paper provides an update on construction of the instrument. It discusses the fabrication and integration of several completed subsystems including the optical bench, vacuum chamber, major optical subassemblies, the Clay front end, electrical systems, and fixturing.

Items.Authors: Amelia Calderhead, Anna MacIver, David Isherwood, Andy Born, James Stevenson
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: Developing a Modular Review Process using TRIZ
Items.Abstract: The HARMONI team at UKATC have been pioneering the use of TRIZ by managing monthly TRIZ workshops to tackle significant project problems that arise. This TRIZ case study investigates how design changes of HARMONI can be reviewed effectively and efficiently. It draws on how the review process of Ground Based Astronomy projects can be improved to add quality to the successful creation of an instrument while reducing strain on designers and reviewer’s time.   To address resource-intensive and document-driven review processes, the case study utilised TRIZ techniques including; thinking in time & scale technique: the 40 inventive principles to tackle design contradiction: function analysis and size, time, cost analysis.  The solution developed considered a modular, continuous review process focusing on specific subsystems or technical topics as they mature while encouraging a live review culture, where stakeholders and expert reviewers are engaged continuously through informal check-ins.

Items.Authors: Paula Bañares-Palacios, Miguel Ángel Cagigas, Alejandro Antonio Luján González, Begoña García-Lorenzo, Ángel Alonso, Adriana de Lorenzo-Cáceres
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: Integral field spectrograph Pre-Optics (IPO) design after rescope process.
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.     The instrument faced budgetary constraints that led to a reduction in the number of available scales in the IPO subsystem. An overview of the process and final design is presented, where 4x4mas, 10x10mas, 20x20mas and 60x30mas scales (in addition to the pupil imaging scale for alignment, which was preserved) were substituted by 6x6mas and 25x25mas scales, compromising technical requirements and scientific needs.

Items.Authors: Rafael Melgar Hernandez, Yolanda Martin, Elvio Hernández Suárez, Alejandro Antonio Luján González, Alberto Hernández González, Horacio Rodriguez Delgado, Felix Gracia Témich, Miguel Angel Cágigas García, Ángel Alonso, Adriana de Lorenzo Cáceres, Begoña García Lorenzo
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: laboratory tests for optimization and validation of the Scale Changer Turret mechanism
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.    This paper reports on the comprehensive testing campaign of the HARMONI IFS Pre-Optic’s (IPO) Scale Changer Turret (SCT) prototype. The primary aim of these tests was to validate the proposed mechanical solution and confirm the overall system performance. We present a detailed analysis of the system and the laboratory setup.

Items.Authors: Eduard R. Muslimov, Matthias Tecza, Edgar Castillo-Domínguez, James Kariuki, Liam Boland, Miriam Cisneros Gonzalez, Kieran McCall, Sophie Paszynska
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: optical design of the spectrograph sub-system
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The University of Oxford is in charge of the design and development of the four identical spectrographs that disperse the light and form scientific images. During the instrument rescope phase, we have developed a new spectrograph optical design. It uses a two-mirror unobscured freeform collimator, a set of volume-phase holographic gratings and grisms as the disperser, and a two-mirror unobscured freeform camera. This design is up to 350 mm shorter than the previous version. The number of optical elements' positioning parameters is reduced by more than two times. The expected as-built minimum transmission is 62.3%, while the scattered light level is decreased.

Items.Authors: Vladislavs Plesanovs, Paolo Soffitta, Hemanth Manikantan, Daniel Saueraland, Klaus Desch, Jochen Kaminski, Carlo Lefevre, Ettore Del Monte
Items.Title: Heavy ion irradiation of GridPix gas detector: a step forward for its use in space
Items.Abstract: The GridPix technology is a candidate to be used as a polarimeter on the potential successor  of IXPE, the EXPO or Enhanced X-ray Polarimetry Observatory. Dedicated set of runs was performed at Bonn Isochronous Cyclotron at HISKP, University of Bonn, to test heavy ion influence in MeV energy range. In a gasseous detector these particles induce overwhelming amount of charge that can saturate the electronics readout or induce sparks and rapidly age the detector. GridPix was subjected to two test beams at a low rate, proton beam at 14MeV and 100MeV 14N5++ ions. The GridPix detector contains the readout ASIC, Timepix, with 256 × 256 pixel grid with a pitch of 55 μm and covered with a protection layer plus gas. The Al grid stands on the SU8 pillars above pixels forming the amplification stage enabling primary electron detection. We describes the setup and results of these tests. The observed impact of irradiation is shown for both types of beam.

Items.Authors: Robert Conwell, Stephen S. Eikenberry, Peter Delfyett, Anish Roshi, Shahebul Hasan, Jiabao Li, Jordan Richey, David Smith, Thuy Nguyen
Items.Title: Heliocomb: a laser frequency comb heterodyne spectrometer for R=200,000,000,000 solar observations
Items.Abstract: We demonstrate a near-infrared heterodyne instrument which achieves a signal-to-noise ratio sufficient for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). VLBI in the near-infrared, achieved by means of heterodyne systems, has the potential to enable ground-based diffraction-limited resolution of millimeter-sized objects in low Earth orbit. Our instrumental design employs an electro-optically modulated laser frequency comb (LFC) as a single-frequency local oscillator with tunability enabled by a calibrated linear stage. Our design is conducive to an instrument with the long-term stability of a LFC, a tunable local oscillator, and scalability for broad instantaneous bandwidth. To demonstrate the efficacy of our instrument, we perform heterodyne spectroscopy on the Sun to measure the Solar Gravitational Redshift, improve upon the current best measurement, and demonstrate year-timescale instrumental stability. This is an essential first step towards near-infrared VLBI.

Items.Authors: Manon Lizzana, Fabien Malbet, Hugo Rousset, Sébastien Soler, Fabrice Pancher
Items.Title: High precision differential astrometry
Items.Abstract: Differential astrometry measures the position and motion of celestial objects relative to nearby stars. Missions like Hipparcos and Gaia reached microarcsecond precision, and future missions such as NASA’s HWO and ESA’s Theia aim for sub-microarcsecond accuracy, enabling studies of Galactic dark matter and the detection of Earth-mass exoplanets.    This work presents key elements of a high-precision astrometric instrument and the simulations of the calibrations required to reach this accuracy. We characterize the 46Mpx Gigapyx CMOS detector from Pyxalis, showing its strong potential for future astrometric focal planes. Sub-microarcsecond precision corresponds to 10⁻⁵ (HWO) or 10⁻⁶ (Theia) pixels on the detector. It requires micro-pixel mapping of gigapixel-scale detectors and optical distortion calibration thanks to high-order polynomial models. We introduce the IPAG (Grenoble) testbed enabling these measurements.

Items.Authors: Chris Hamner, Sébastien Vievard, Akinyele Gilbert, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: High resolution Echelle Spectrometer integrating 19 channel photonic lantern
Items.Abstract: In exoplanet science, high-resolution spectroscopy enables the identification of companions with narrow emission lines and the isolation of giant exoplanets, as well as facilitating the measurements of orbital velocities, masses, and molecular signatures. We aim to develop a high-throughput spectro-imaging solution that simultaneously provides the benefits of single mode fiber (SMF)-spectroscopy, and accesses spatial and spectral information below the telescope diffraction limit. We propose a design for a single mode Echelle spectrometer that accepts simultaneous input from a photonic lantern (PL) having 19 single mode fiber (SMF) outputs. In addition to the 19 SMF input channels, the spectrometer is designed to separate each channel into linear polarization states, resulting in 46 spectral measurements (38 stellar channels and 8 calibration channels). The design and fabrication status for the spectrometer will be presented.

Items.Authors: Bhushan Joshi, Nicolas Erasmus, Willem Smit, Anamparambu N. Ramaprakash, Hitesh Gajjar, Kathryn Rosie
Items.Title: High-cadence, AI-assisted sCMOS camera for time-domain astronomy
Items.Abstract: We propose a small, AI-assisted sCMOS camera designed for quick transient detection. The system combines an NVIDIA Jetson Orin module, scalable FPGA control circuits, and a low-noise sCMOS sensor to carry out CNN-based transient classification and real-time image correction at the telescope. This local operation reduces latency and data transfer. Designed with adaptability in mind, the architecture can be extended to support upcoming astronomical applications such as multi-detector arrays or CubeSat-based instruments.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Calvin, Michael Fitzgerald, Jessica Castellanos
Items.Title: High-contrast aperture masking interferometry: using a vortex coronagraph for detecting companions within the diffraction limit
Items.Abstract: The search for the direct discovery of exoplanets has motivated high-contrast imaging surveys using coronagraphs with narrow inner working angles. Traditional imaging methods are limited by the size of the on-axis PSF and are not sensitive to companions at close separations. Meanwhile, non-redundant masking (NRM) techniques are used with single-aperture telescopes to resolve astrophysical features within the diffraction limit, but NRM interferometry faces sensitivity issues at high contrasts. In these proceedings, we investigate simulations utilizing high contrast coronagraphy in conjunction with NRM interferometry. The vortex coronagraph delivers an improvement in the relative throughput of a close-separation companion, which improves the sensitivity of the interferometric observables. This preliminary investigation introduces the conceptual architecture for combining these techniques and explores the potential discovery space for high contrast targets within the diffraction limit.

Items.Authors: Quan Zhang
Items.Title: High-precision image stabilization control strategy for large space astronomical telescope
Items.Abstract: The precision image stabilization subsystem of the large space astronomical telescope usually incorporates a fast steering mirror(FSM) and several fine guide sensors (FGS). The Fine Guide Sensor, serving as the detection module of the precision stabilization system, is located at the edge of the main field of view and shares the primary optical system with the main focal plane. The FGS first carries out the high-frame-rate star target extraction and positioning, then calculates these extracted star points to output both relative attitude information (line-of-sight deviation of the space telescope) and absolute attitude information (three-axis orientation of the telescope). The piezoelectric-driven large-aperture fast steering mirror, serving as the actuator in the precision image stabilization system, is responsible for compensating line-of-sight deviations and fine pointing adjustment.

Items.Authors: Yuyao Liu, Yonghui Hou, Teng Xu, Jiangfang Hua, Xuhao Wu, Wei Wei, Chao Liu, Yue Sun, Hang Zhang
Items.Title: High-stability vacuum delay line for optical interferometry: mechanical deformation analysis and optical performance evaluation
Items.Abstract: We present a study on the mechanical and optical performance of a high-stability vacuum delay line designed for optical interferometry. The system operates under a moderate vacuum level of 10⁻³ atm and aims to ensure structural rigidity and stable optical propagation. Finite element and optical modeling were used to evaluate the deformation behavior and resulting wavefront quality. The results indicate that the delay line maintains sufficient stability for interferometric applications, demonstrating its suitability for future extensions toward longer delay strokes and enhanced measurement precision.

Items.Authors: Giovanni Della Casa, Francesco Ceraudo, Ettore Del Monte, Giuseppe Dilillo, Marco Feroci, Edoardo Giancarli, Alessio Nuti, Riccardo Campana, Mauro Fiorini, Giovanni Lombardi, Massimo Rapisarda, Ajay Sharma, Giuseppe Bertuccio, Filippo Mele, Yinhe Zhu, Marco Grassi, Piero Malcovati, Jacopo Giani, Marco Tambussi, Matias Antonelli, Alexander Rachevski, Irina Rashevskaya, Gianluigi Zampa, Nicola Zampa, Evgeny Demenev, Giancarlo Pepponi, Francesco Ficorella, Nicola Zorzi
Items.Title: High-throughput spectral-timing with large-area SDDs
Items.Abstract: The Large Area Detector (LAD) is an instrument concept based on an array of collimated large-area linear Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs). Its design was specifically developed to perform optimal spectral resolution and timing studies in the 2-30 keV band. A prototype of LAD with lower number of anodes was coupled with a novel CMOS analog front-end Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (AFE ASIC), named NOVA, to demonstrate the performances of the combined instruments, in view of future mission proposals. In this work, we will present the spectral resolution results obtained for the integrated detector system (NOVA ASIC and SDD prototype) as a function of operational parameters.

Items.Authors: Maxime Lebreton
Items.Title: HIRIS, the low-noise and high dynamic hyperspectral imager project
Items.Abstract: Short-wave infrared wavelength imaging (SWIR, between 900 to 1700 nm) opens our vision below the visible spectrum. This presentation introduces HIRIS, a hyperspectral imager project based on SIRIS, a fast, low-noise and high dynamic range SWIR camera. Using a cold tunable filter avoids influence of black body radiation at ambient temperature (300 K) and allows low signal sensitivity during hyperspectral acquisition. It will first be discussed. The presentation will also be focused on tunable filter selection and modeling. The chosen Fabry-Perot interferometer on a electronically and mechanically constrained device will be explained. To conclude, early results obtained with the first HIRIS prototype will be detailed, as well of associated data processing and scientific outlooks.

Items.Authors: Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, Charles Kilpatrick, Bryson Cale, Ben Sappey, Ashley Baker, Max Brodheim, Don Neill, Samuel Halverson, Quinn Konopacky, Charles Beichman, Graham Bruce Berriman, Rob Bertz, Ava DeLaGarza, Jocelyn Ferrara, Luke Finnerty, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Aidan Gibbs, Rose Gibson, Katelyn Horstman, Nemanja Jovanovic, Marc Kassis, Stephanie Leifer, Andrea Lin, Jeff Mader, Dimitri Mawet, Jason Wang
Items.Title: HISPEC data reduction pipeline II: H4RG detector calibrations and up-the-ramp data processing
Items.Abstract: HISPEC is a new high-resolution spectrograph (R>100k) currently being built for the W.M. Keck Observatory with simultaneous 0.98-2.5 μm wavelength range coverage. HISPEC is equipped with two H4RG-10 detectors which were spares of the Roman Space Telescope. We will describe the first stage of the HISPEC data reduction pipeline (stage 0) which aims at processing the up-the-ramp data to generate fully calibrated electron rate maps. The pipeline needs to be both extremely accurate to enable precise radial velocity measurements (<30 cm/s) and computationally efficient to continuously process the multiple terra-bytes of data generated per day with HISPEC.

Items.Authors: Davide Ricci, Simone Doniselli, Lorenzo Cabona, Davide Greggio, Matteo Aliverti, Silvano Tosi
Items.Title: How to turn a small observatory into a multi-instrument facility for photometry, long slit, and échelle spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Observatories of class up to 1m are commonly provided with COTS cameras for imaging/photometry. This is especially true for didactic, outreach, and private telescopes, although they are also successfully used for scientific purposes.  Spectroscopy is generally relegated to larger, institutional facilities and their corresponding professional instruments. However, semi-professional solutions exist. How to integrate them in small observatories?  We present the first light of Cerberus, a three-headed instrument for the 80cm OARPAF telescope in Northern Italy: a new Nashmyth interface flange allows connecting not only the existing SBIG CCD camera, but also a LHIRESIII long slit and a FLECHAS échelle spectrograph. Moreover, the photometry mode is upgraded with a tip-tilt lens to correct for tracking and vibrations at a 10Hz rate.  The three instruments are alternatively selected through a linear stage provided with mirrors, and are remotely operated by a custom web-based graphical interface.

Items.Authors: Chao Tang, Arwa Dabbech, Adrian Jackson, Yves Wiaux
Items.Title: HyperAIRI: a plug-and-play algorithm for precise hyperspectral image reconstruction in radio interferometry
Items.Abstract: Next-generation radio interferometers will produce extremely large, wideband observations that require precise and scalable imaging methods. We present HyperAIRI, a new hyperspectral imaging algorithm designed to meet this demand by combining optimization theory and deep learning, with an overall algorithmic convergence guarantee. HyperAIRI alternates a data-fidelity step with a regularization step via learned hyperspectral deep-neural-network denoisers. Each spectral channel is processed in parallel using denoisers matched to its dynamic range, informed by its neighboring channels and a physically motivated power-law spectral model. A shelf of networks spanning typical dynamic ranges provides further flexibility. Tests on simulated and real observations show that HyperAIRI delivers state-of-the-art imaging precision compared with existing optimization-based and CLEAN-based approaches, while preserving the efficiency of the monochromatic AIRI framework.

Items.Authors: Luca Girolimetto, Emanuele Simioni, Claudio Pernechele, Giovanni Costa, Paolo Martini, Luigi Lessio, Adriano Tullo, Cristina Re, Matteo Massironi, Diego Scaccabarozzi, Leonardo Amoruso, Carmela Agnese De Donno, Marco Mucci Beltrami, Alessandro Varriale
Items.Title: Hyper-hemispherical structure from motion for lunar cave exploration
Items.Abstract: The paper presents "HH-SfM" (Hyper-Hemispherical Structure from Motion) a global structure-from-motion algorithm developed for the ESA Daedalus mission to explore and map Moon caves using a robot with a hyper-hemispherical lens system. The goal is to reconstruct the robot’s trajectory and environment during its descent into a lava tube. The system’s rig consists of four cameras, allowing each cave point to be seen by at least three cameras. The algorithm optimizes the rig's position and triangulated points using a global bundle adjustment, incorporating odometry for scale correction. The resulting geometry enables photogrammetric reconstruction for geological analysis and exploration of Moon channels, with potential applications on Earth.

Items.Authors: Christian Eredia, Vincenzo Cianniello, Enrico Cascone
Items.Title: Implementation of extended reality in the development process of astronomical instrumentation
Items.Abstract: An eXtended Reality (XR) laboratory has been created in the Astronomical Observatory of Capodimonte, in Naples, in the scope of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan project "STILES - Strengthening the Italian leadership in ELT and SKA".  The laboratory is supporting the design process of the new generation of astronomical instrumentation. An upgrade of the XR equipment has already taken place, with the aim of building multi-user sessions, which prove to be extremely useful both for design reviews and especially for training and testing maintance operations.  The laboratory has been transferred to its ultimate location, in the Naples Concurrent Design Facility, where the XR technologies have been paired with the tools already installed in the facility, starting also to support the first concurrent design sessions.   This paper describes both the upgrades made on the hardware side, and the activities that are being carried out by exploiting the acquired techonologies.

Items.Authors: Paul Rabe, Carel van Gend, Nicolas Erasmus, Stephen Potter
Items.Title: Implementing telemetry as part of the SAAO Intelligent Observatory initiative
Items.Abstract: This work describes the development of a unified telemetry system for the SAAO Intelligent Observatory initiative. The system collects real-time operational data, including environmental metrics, subsystem states, logs, and audio streams, and ingests them into a central FastAPI-based service with PostgreSQL storage. PyTorch-based autoencoders perform real-time audio anomaly detection, and operators access dashboards for system status, spectrograms, and alerts. A standard JSON telemetry format ensures consistent data submission while requiring only minor client-side adaptations for each subsystem. Lightweight acquisition nodes, including Raspberry Pi devices, capture and forward local telemetry. All software components are open-source, free from licensing restrictions, and supported by active development communities. The system provides improved situational awareness, increased automation, and supports predictive maintenance across SAAO facilities.

Items.Authors: Michael R. Vissers, Logan Howe, Andrea Giachero, Pietro Campana, Corwin Shiu, Maya Erickson, Jordan Wheeler, Johannes Hubmayr, Joel Ullom
Items.Title: Improved inverted microstrip kinetic inductance traveling wave amplifiers for detector array readout
Items.Abstract: Kinetic inductance traveling wave (KIT) parametric amplifiers based on NbTiN have demonstrated gain >20dB across several gigahertz of usable bandwidth, added noise of less than a photon more than the quantum limit. and sufficient dynamic range to read out large numbers of superconducting resonators. However, difficulties in integration into readout chains suitable for large arrays of devices have limited their impact. Here, we discuss significant progress on improving the design, microwave launch, microwave ground, as well as replacing the previously needed bulky, lossy, commercial components with superconducting on-chip replacements. These improvements result in high performance devices with beyond octave bandwidth that are far more compact and show reduced gain ripple and insertion loss than previous iterations. We will also discuss preliminary results on scaling the amplification bandwidth to higher (>20GHz) and lower (1GHz) frequency bands.

Items.Authors: Masaki Numazawa, Manabu Ishida, Yuichiro Ezoe, Naoya Sera, Ryo Kishikawa, Atsuto Matsumura, Mai Takeo, Asca Miyamoto, Tsubasa Uchino, Kumi Ishikawa, Yoshitomo Maeda, Daiki Ishi, Kohei Morishita, Kazuo Nakajima
Items.Title: Improvement of imaging performance of silicon foil X-ray optics using hot plastic deformation process
Items.Abstract: We have been developing silicon foil X-ray optics using hot plastic deformation for future astronomical observations. A 0.3-mm-thick silicon wafer was formed into a precise conical shape with a curvature radius of ~100 mm. Owing to the favorable physical properties of silicon, these mirrors offer reduced weight and improved angular resolution compared to conventional aluminum foil optics. Process optimization achieved an angular resolution of 27.4 arcseconds along the best generatrix—a twofold improvement over previous results—evaluated at the ISAS/JAXA 30-m X-ray beamline. This paper presents fabrication improvements and enhanced X-ray imaging performance of the silicon foil optics.

Items.Authors: Gianluca Marotta, Matteo Di Carlo, Stefano Di Frischia, Elisabetta Giani
Items.Title: Improving observability and reliability in SKA Control Software through TANGO-Controls Open Telemetry and CSP.LMC Test Analytics
Items.Abstract: In the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) project, early detection of rare and hard-to-reproduce anomalies is essential to ensure system reliability. SKA software components, built on TANGO-Controls and deployed as Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, can exhibit unpredictable or non-deterministic behaviour that must be closely monitored. To improve insight into such failures, the Central Signal Processor Local Monitoring and Control (CSP.LMC) subsystem has begun collecting detailed test-failure statistics and benchmarking data. With the introduction of OpenTelemetry support in TANGO-Controls, new observability capabilities have become available. This work explores how combining Tango OpenTelemetry instrumentation with CSP.LMC’s test-result collection framework can enhance anomaly detection, strengthen performance benchmarking, and improve software quality across the SKA ecosystem.

Items.Authors: Ryan J. Oelkers, Luke Schmidt, Moises Castillo, Erika Cook, Richard Camuccio, Eric Gonzalez, Carlos Francile, Mario Diaz, Diego G. Lambas, Lucas Macri, Darren DePoy, Jennifer Marshall, Federico Podesta, Ricardo Podesta
Items.Title: Infrastructure and instrument upgrades in support of the Transient Optical Robotic Observatory of the South (TOROS) at the Felix Aguilar Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Transient Optical Robotic Observatory of the South (TOROS) is a newly commissioned ground-based observatory deployed to the Felix Aguilar Observatory based out of the Carlos Ulrrico Cesco Astronomical Station in San Juan, Argentina. TOROS was designed to provide optical follow-up of potential gravitational wave sources, and a planned upgrade during the spring of 2026 will enable TOROS to obtain rapid response color observations for transient events and variable stars discovered by the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Rubin-LSST). Here we report on the planned infrastructure and instrument upgrades to modernize the Felix Aguilar Observatory including our plans for the full robotization of the facility, on-site automatic data reduction, and integration into several alert streams. The observatory has already achieved first light, and we expect full operations to start in the summer of 2026 to coincide with the first year of Rubin-LSST operations.

Items.Authors: Juan Francisco Hernández Cabrera, Carlos Colodro-Conde, Xana Delpueyo Español
Items.Title: In-orbit temporal stability analysis of the DRAGO-2 SWIR imager: quantifying radiometric and spatial variability using lunar targets
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a temporal stability analysis of the DRAGO-2 SWIR imager's performance, using imagery of the Moon captured in-orbit. Spatial stability (MTF, FWHM) is tracked via cross-validated slanted-edge and lunar-limb methods. Absolute radiometric stability is quantified using multiple full-moon acquisitions and the LIME model. This work introduces a correction for detector-plane scattering using a K0 Bessel-function model. The analysis provides valuable data on instrument degradation, critical for validating design choices for future SWIR space instrumentation and guaranteeing the fidelity of Level 2 scientific data products.

Items.Authors: Mia R. Lilley, David Buscher
Items.Title: In-situ pixel mapping in extreme precision RV spectrographs
Items.Abstract: The detection of Earth twins will be one of the major stepping-stones in our search for life in the Universe. One of the most promising avenues to make these detections is through the use of extreme precision radial velocity methods to allow the detection of stellar reﬂex signals at the 10 cm/s level typical for an Earth twin. Achieving long-term radial velocity precisions at these levels will require spectrographs where the wavelength corresponding to each detector pixel is known to precisions considerably better than a part in a billion. We use a new calibration method that enables us to map the positions of all the illuminated pixels in the spectrograph. Unlike conventional pixel-mapping techniques, our method can be done in-situ in the spectrograph, so any detector distortions which occur during the spectrograph's lifetime can be measured and accounted for. We discuss our ongoing programme to develop this technique to achieve such precisions and present our preliminary results.

Items.Authors: Ross Cheriton, Emma Rautio-Roe, Glen Herriot, Alexis Hill, Brent Carlson, Siegfried Janz, Thushara Gunaratne, Zoran Ljusic, John Weber, Martin Vachon, Shurui Wang, Nicaulas Sabourin, Jianhao Zhang, Dan-Xia Xu, Pavel Cheben, Jens H. Schmid
Items.Title: Integrated silicon photonics for long baseline optical aperture synthesis
Items.Abstract: Optical aperture synthesis is the most promising route towards achieving the very high spatial resolution required to resolve features on exoplanets themselves. However, the required baselines are on the order of tens of kilometers, which makes phasing each receiver extremely challenging in the optical regime. Integrated photonics can provide a scalable and stable platform for optical beamforming that can compensate for atmospheric turbulence. We outline our experimental progress towards a photonic aperture synthesis proof-of-concept instrument which uses a photonic integrated circuit to achieve coherent phasing and combination of light from multiple receivers.

Items.Authors: Nyasha Suliali, James M. Ivory, Konstantin D. Stefanov, David Hall, Manish R. Patel
Items.Title: Integrated UV and optical scientific CMOS sensor characterisation with in-built quality control
Items.Abstract: Electro-optical characterisation of a scientific CMOS sensor has been demonstrated. Characterisation of the sensor in the 200 to 400 nm wavelength region, on an integrated bench setup with a single control panel has been demonstrated. This paper outlines the construction, calibration and integration of the supervisory, control, data acquisition, processing and reporting functions on a single platform for seamless sensor characterisation. Critical characterisation aspects such as in-built sub-system quality control, total test duration and measurements of selected parameters such as the system read noise, dark current and photo response from 20 °C down to -25 °C are presented.
